title: The time of Vespasian
hookLine: picture Vespasian's age: marrying, farming, flattering, all gone (Meditations 4.32)
last: ASK WHO ACTUALLY NEEDS ME NOW.

lines: A PHOTO OF YOUR STREET, 100 YEARS AGO.
EVERYONE IN IT, IN A HURRY.
cards: Find an old photograph of your street from about a hundred years ago. A man in a hat hurrying somewhere. Two women talking outside a shop.
A boy with a bicycle. Each of them was in the middle of something urgent: a debt, a crush, a quarrel with a brother. Every one of those urgencies is finished now.
Marcus Aurelius did this exercise without photographs, using an emperor from an earlier generation of Rome.

teach.h: THINK OF THE TIMES OF VESPASIAN.
teach.b: Think of the times of Vespasian, Marcus writes in book four, entry thirty-two. Vespasian was an emperor from before Marcus's time. And what do you see?

People marrying, raising children, getting sick, dying, fighting wars, feasting, trading, farming, flattering, being stubbornly proud, suspecting, plotting, wishing others dead, grumbling at the present, loving, piling up treasure, longing for high office and for power.
Everything people did then, and do now.
And that whole life of theirs, Marcus says, no longer exists anywhere. Then he does it again with the emperor Trajan's time, a little closer. Same list.
Also gone. He isn't doing this to feel gloomy or superior. He's doing it to measure.
The quarrel that feels enormous this week is the same size as the quarrels in Vespasian's Rome. Look, he says, at how many threw themselves into these things, and then fell, and came apart.
What lasts, for him, is not the outcome of the hurry. It's whether, in the middle of it, a person kept to what is right.

teach.h: IT SHRINKS THE HURRY, NOT THE GOOD.
teach.b: The exercise shrinks the hurry, not the good.
The worries get smaller. Character doesn't.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes picture their own town a century ago, as in Meditations 4.32, to see their present worries at their true size.

o: the emperor Marcus served under as a young man
the emperor whose age Marcus pictures, now all gone
a Roman god of time and of things passing

p: the second, closer age Marcus pictures

s: Marcus pictures only the great deeds of Vespasian's age
his list is ordinary life: marrying, farming, grumbling, plotting.
Marcus repeats the exercise with Trajan's time
a little closer, the same list, also gone.
the exercise is meant to make Marcus feel superior
it's for measuring: his own worries are the same size as theirs.

games.q: you're losing sleep over who gets the corner office. what would Marcus's exercise in 4.32 do?
o: make the fight feel more important.
picture it in Vespasian's Rome, and let it shrink.
tell you to win at any cost.
games.why: Marcus's list includes longing for office and power. all of it, he says, is gone. what remains is how you behaved.

practice: Picture the place you live a century ago: the same ground, different buildings, people walking and worrying, each one sure their worry was the big one. Then set one worry of your own among them, and notice its size there.

wordCard.voice: Vespasian. Marcus pictures Vespasian's Rome, marrying, farming, flattering, plotting, and notes that all of it is gone. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the emperor Vespasian, whose age Marcus pictures first in 4.32.

carryVoice: Your line: all gone. Every urgency in that old photograph has finished. See you tomorrow.
